title: Seattle Times and Newsday sue OpenAI and Microsoft over training-data copying
subtitle: The two papers ask the Southern District of New York to order the impoundment or destruction of any AI model built on their journalism.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: The Seattle Times and Newsday filed a joint copyright suit against OpenAI and Microsoft in the US District Court for the Southern District of New York on September 4, and the docket became public September 5. The complaint alleges the two companies scraped both papers' websites — including content behind paywalls — and used the articles to train and operate ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot, and Bing's AI features. It seeks unspecified damages and court orders requiring the impoundment or destruction of any training dataset or model that incorporates the papers' work.

The suit also brings a trademark claim: it alleges OpenAI's outputs sometimes attribute fabricated material to the Seattle Times and Newsday by name, diluting the papers' brands and misleading readers about what those newsrooms actually published. That claim is legally narrower than the copyright count but tactically important — trademark dilution has a clearer damages theory than statutory copyright when the plaintiff cannot prove specific commercial loss.

The filing is the second cluster of publisher litigation in three months. In late June, a coalition of nearly 400 local newspapers filed a similar mass action; that case is still in early motions. The New York Times case from December 2023 is now approaching two years and remains the anchor precedent every subsequent filing cites. What is changing is the remedy: newer complaints, including this one, explicitly ask for model destruction rather than only damages — the same relief AI labs have been quietly settling to avoid.

For learners: the legal question in these suits is not whether training on copyrighted text is happening — the labs concede it — but whether it is fair use. That is a fact-specific inquiry courts make one case at a time, and the answers are still being written. Follow the Southern District of New York docket for the New York Times case; whatever standard emerges there will shape every AI copyright claim filed after it, this one included.
